Alexander Glasgow of Old Court, County Cork, formerly of Auchenraith, Lanarkshire, died at Old Court on 19 October 1873; the printed Irish probate calendar records his will proved at Cork on 10 December 1873 by Robert Pirrie, one of the executors, with effects under £80,000. sections.title: Source findings
sections.markdown:
### Findmypast sweep — 7 October 2026

- **New: burial.** Ffolliott collection, Douglas parish (Cork & Ross), **burial of Alexander Glasgow, 24 October 1873** (`IRE/FFOLLIOTT/REG/145696`).
- **New: estate notice naming the executor and date of death.** *Cork Constitution*, 9 January 1874, p.1 (`BL/0001648/18740109/009`, OCR read): statutory notice to creditors of "Alexander Glasgow, late of Oldcourt, in the county of Cork, Esquire, deceased, who died on the 19th day of October, 1873"; claims to the solicitor for "Robert Pirrie, the executor", probate granted in the Cork District Registry. The Original Will Register entry (Cork District Will Books, May 1873–Dec 1874, images 007604247_00158–00166, `IRE/ORIG/WILL/REG/15268`) indexes the names associated with the grant as "Robert Shan", "Edward Eyre", "Robert Pissie" and "John Pinie" — probably Robert Shaw, Edward Eyre [Newenham], Robert Pirrie and John Pirrie, but these readings need the image; the will itself was not read.
- **New: death notices in Scotland.** *Greenock Advertiser*, 23 October 1873 (index `FN-D-2F174051-...`, article `BL/0000970/18731023/002`) is indexed with death 19 October 1873 at Cork, **aged 81** (index fields; page OCR not read); *North British Daily Mail*, 21 October 1873 (`BL/0002683/18731021/066`); *Cork Constitution*, 21 October 1873 (`BL/0001648/18731021/002`; snippet: "at his residence, Old Court, county Cork, Alexander Glasgow, Esq."). Also indexed: Death Duty Register index, 1873, IR 27/385 (`BMD/D/DDUTY/1357936`); Great Western Railway shareholder register, death 19 October 1873 (`GBOR/GWR/00051801`).
- **New: widow's death.** *Western Morning News*, 22 December 1873, p.1 (`BL/0000329/18731222/001`, OCR read): "At Old Court, county of [Cork] ... widow of the late Alexander Glasgow, in her 79th year." Her forename and the day are illegible in the OCR. The age (born about 1794–95) is compatible with Ellen Smith, but the notice as read does not name her.
- **New: only son and only daughter in contemporary notices.** *Southern Reporter*, 2 August 1855, p.2 (`BL/0000876/18550802/060`): on 31 July at Monkstown Church, "William James Glasgow, Esq., **only son** of Alexander Glasgow, Esq., of Old Court, to Dora, eldest daughter of Bernard H. Shaw, Esq., of Monkstown." *Dublin Evening Mail*, 10 June 1853, p.3 (`BL/0000433/18530610/043`): 7 June at Douglas, Edward Eyre Newenham of Maryborough to "Jessy, **only daughter** of Alexander Glasgow, Esq., of Old Court, county of Cork, late of Auchenraith, Lanarkshire." The 1855 notice conflicts with the profile's third child, John: by 1855 William James was the only living son, so John, if he existed, had probably died. The 1853 notice directly links the Cork man to Auchenraith.
- **New (context):** Old Court gate-lodge was attacked by Fenians seeking arms in mid-March 1868 (the reports differ between Sunday night and Monday morning), "the residence of Alexander Glasgow, Esq., a magistrate" (*Dublin Evening Mail*, 19 March 1868, `BL/0000433/18680319/042`, and widely reprinted). Directories: Henry & Coughlan 1867, Douglas (`IRE/IET0012/367/017`); Slater 1870, Cork (`IRE/IET0100/0646/054`).
- **Not a record of him:** Findmypast's "Irish Newspaper Marriage Notices" entry for Alexander Glasgow, Cork Examiner, 20 November 1854 (`FN-M-DE3EE6D2-...`) is a misindexed one-guinea subscription to the South Infirmary, not a marriage.
- **New Zealand (family, not him):** *Lyttelton Times*, 29 November 1889 (`BL/0003346/18891129/038`): Francis Bernard, "fourth son of the late William James Glasgow, of Old Court, County Cork, Ireland, and Brooklands, Nelson, New Zealand", married Marisa Victorine Malfroy at Hokitika on 20 November 1889. Landed Estates Court sale notices of 1891 (e.g. *Irish Times*, 27 March 1891, `BL/0001683/18910327/149`) name Robert Pirrie as administrator of William James Glasgow, deceased, in the Newenham estate case. No New Zealand record of Alexander himself was found (Findmypast NZ index: only an 1874 birth and 1880 marriage of other Alexanders).

sections.title: Source findings — 1873 probate calendar entry, 10 December 1873
sections.markdown:
The printed Irish *Calendar of Wills and Administrations* for 1873 (right-hand page of the pp. 246–247 opening; an image of the opening is kept in the owner's old research archive) reads: "GLASGOW Alexander. 10 December. The Will of Alexander Glasgow late of Old Court County Cork Esquire deceased who died 19 October 1873 at same place was proved at Cork by the oath of Robert Pirrie of West George-street Glasgow Esquire one of the Executors. Effects under £80,000."

Seen as an image of the printed calendar, read by on-device OCR and checked against the column layout. Grade: proved for the death date and place, the grant at Cork on 10 December 1873 and Robert Pirrie's role as one of the executors. The calendar gives £80,000 as the upper limit of the sworn effects; it does not support the captured biography's statement that Alexander left £80,000 to Robert Pirrie. The will itself has not been read, so the legatees are unknown.

On 14 September 1795 John Glasgow, merchant, entered as husband of Helen, lawful daughter of James Smith, mason and burgess/guild brother (printed p.197, PDF 207). On 1 July 1817 Alexander Glasgow, merchant in Wilson’s Court, Argyle Street, entered as eldest son of John Glasgow, merchant and burgess/guild brother (p.306, PDF 316). On 3 May 1844 John Glasgow, merchant, entered as a younger son of John Glasgow, merchant and burgess/guild brother (p.450, PDF 460). The first entry strongly identifies the maintained John-1348/Helen Smith household; the sons are supported comparisons with Alexander-971 and John-1355. The sons’ entries do not name their mother, and the three admissions must not be treated as a literal statement that all three men form one family. These are inspected published register transcriptions; the underlying manuscript admission registers are unread.

Burke’s Visitation, vol.2, printed armorial section p.67 (PDF 341), has now been read in the scan. It explicitly describes Alexander of Old Court, formerly Auchinraith, as eldest son of the late John Glasgow and Helen, daughter of James Smith, and grandson of Alexander Glasgow, merchant, and Agnes Monro of Edinburgh. The family passage was already quoted in the held biography; inspecting it is not discovery of a previously unknown grandfather name. The underlying Lyon matriculation remains unread.

The FamilySearch citation X17D-67M was checked directly: John was born 13 October 1771 and christened 19 October 1771 at Barony, parents Alexander Glasgow and Mary Munro. The copied 3 December 1765 date attached to that same citation is wrong; no independent 1765 record was verified in this review. This corrects the source account, not the vital fields or later identity of either modern John profile.

The independently identified John–Helen Smith merchant household now has inspected burgess evidence, and Burke explicitly gives its Alexander grandfather with a Monro wife associated with Edinburgh. That rare paired family description is more specific than the earlier chronological comparison with Alexander-1309’s Alexander/Mary Munro household, whose 1757 marriage was recorded in Edinburgh and Barony. The corrected 1771 Barony child fits the merchant’s possible generation. This modestly strengthens the whole existing father-profile hypothesis from 38% to 45% Possible; it does not make it Probable. Burke names Agnes Monro, not the documented Mary Munro of Alexander-1309’s couple. Their identity cannot be assumed, and the 1771 child has no inspected occupation, wife or estate bridge identifying him as the merchant rather than the Colinton account John-1304. The merchant’s circa 1770 birth is an inherited estimate, not independent corroboration. Retain both modern Johns and the current father selection, all mothers, vital fields and upstream grades. No new father attachment or merge follows. The 1741 childhood identification of Alexander-1309 is not certified by this review. Exact percentages are subjective judgements, not measured probabilities.

potential_parentage.method: Automated leads use birth surnames—not married surnames—as parental eligibility, role-specific biological age limits, bounded and approximate-date uncertainty, household chronology, specific time-aware localities, mapped distance, tenancy succession, migration destinations and sex-aware Scottish naming positions across generations. People already attached as the subject's parents stay in the identity summary and are excluded from this alternative-candidate list, regardless of relationship confidence. The main calibration uses clues available on disconnected profiles; existing parent and sibling links are retained as comparison context rather than treated as transferable evidence. Common ordered names and grandparent-to-child echoes receive a small non-zero weight, so a John or James match can support several independent criteria without producing a lead alone. Rare names, repeated bearers and bundles across otherwise distinct branches receive substantially more weight according to catalogue frequency. An exact migration place is weighted by its rarity and repetition across both branches; a shared destination country is worth only one point. Extra weight is added only when at least three independent clue types converge: naming, locality, specific migration, household chronology or collateral networks. Sparse profiles retain a clearly labelled chronology-only fallback instead of disappearing. Countries, states, counties and research clusters do not count as a shared locality, and fallback, broad representative or kin-inferred coordinates are excluded from distance scoring. Shared descendant profiles are removed before branch-name comparison. A candidate already recorded as a parent-in-law is excluded. A confident or independently supported parent is treated as settled; uncertain and unassessed attachments remain open to alternative comparison. A different linked parent, an uncle/aunt or grandparent path, and a matching existing child profile prevent an alternative from being classified as a strong direct-parent lead until the underlying tree conflict or duplicate is resolved. Familiar forms such as Bessie are normalised. Surname remains an eligibility filter worth zero points.
potential_parentage.warning: Naming customs, shared farms and occupations are circumstantial. Children, spouses and collateral relatives may be missing, and tree-derived family networks are not independent evidence. Scores rank research leads; they do not prove parentage.

{{One Name Study|name=Glasgow}}
Alexander Glasgow was born on 1 November 1792 (Barony Parish) and was baptised on 5 November 1792.<ref>Email from Alan McGowan, historian for Chess Scotland, researching the history of the Glasgow Chess Club. He notes "club member Robert Pirrie, who is mentioned in your pages, gifted a notice from 1827 that was addressed to 'A. Glasgow, Esq., Messrs. Frew & Glasgow, North Albion Court.' This notice said that 'The Chess Club will meet in the Royal Hotel Georges Square on Monday first the 12th curt., at 7 o'clock Evening .....' and was sent by  Jno. Ross, Secretary." "I had been researching Alexander Glasgow for some time and had found some of the information that was uploaded December 5. For your information, he was born 1 November 1792 (Barony Parish) with baptism on the 5th. He was associated at one point with with Auchinraith, Lanarkshire (sometimes Auchenraith).  

A search of Google Books will bring up entries in Burke's Peerage with the family details, including confirmation of his date of birth."</ref> 

He was a merchant from Lanarkshire in Scotland, who operated under Alexander Glasgow & Co house 201 St Vincent street.

He who bought the Oldcourt estate, county Cork, from the Goolds in 1852. Griffith's Valuation records Alexander Glasgow holding land in the parish of Carrigaline, barony and county of Cork. 

In 1826 Alexander Glasgow married Ellen Smith and they had three children, John, William and Jessy who married Edward Eyre Newenham of Maryborough in 1853. In the 1870s William James Glasgow owned 1,599 acres in county Cork. 

He died in 19 October 1873 in Cork<ref>Civil death record: https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/deaths_returns/deaths_1873/020675/7254517.pdf</ref>, leaving £80,000 to Robert Pirrie.<ref>https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:KZ5W-MGV</ref>. The cause of his death was registered as "Brain disease". 

'''Auchinraith'''
''' - 1852'''

Auchinraith was sold to Alexander Glasgow, merchant in Glasgow, who retired from business and the city a number of years ago, and resided in the South of Ireland. Robert Ker, an old and esteemed citizen of Glasgow, bought it from him in 1852. Mr. Glasgow bought and sold it for about £12,000; when Mr. Ker disposed of it, the price he received was £45,000.

http://www.glasgowwestaddress.co.uk/Old_Country_Houses/Auchinraith.htm

'''Oldcourt'''
'''1852-1901'''

Oldcourt was the seat of the Goold family baronets until 1852 when it was bought by Alexander Glasgow. The sale rental of March 1852 includes a lithograph of Oldcourt. Griffith's Valuation records Glasgow holding the property in fee and the buildings were valued at £68. The Glasgows leased the house until it was bought in the early 20th century by Henry O'Shea although Alexander J. Glasgow is recorded as the occupier in 1906 when it was valued at £51. Henry O'Shea sold it to the Brothers of Charity in 1934 whose services used it as a Special Needs school. It is still extant.

'''Kilmanahan Castle
''''''1852 - 1855'''

Robert Sparrow was leasing this property from the Greene estate in 1850 when it was valued at over £72. It was offered for sale as part of William Greene's estate in July and December 1852. The sale notice includes a lithograph of the castle. It was bought by Alexander Glasgow who sold it on to the Earl of Donoughmore in 1855. Earlier, in 1786, Wilson notes it as the seat of Mr. Greene. In 1837, Lewis refers to it as the seat of Lt. Col. Nuttall Greene. Hussey records Thomas Wright Watson of Kilmanahan Castle in the mid 1870s. In 1906 it was part of th Donoughmore estate and valued at £45. It is still extant.

Mary Lyons records the purchase by Alexander Glasgow of Kilmanahan Castle, county Waterford, in 1852 for £9,400 but shortly afterwards he sold the property on to the Earl of Donoughmore.<ref>https://landedestates.ie/estate/3101</ref>

record_associations.note: The 1935 printed Glasgow burgess register has been visually inspected. On 14 September 1795 John Glasgow, merchant, entered as husband of Helen, lawful daughter of James Smith, mason and burgess/guild brother (printed p.197, PDF 207). On 1 July 1817 Alexander Glasgow, merchant in Wilson’s Court, Argyle Street, entered as eldest son of John Glasgow, merchant and burgess/guild brother (p.306, PDF 316). On 3 May 1844 John Glasgow, merchant, entered as a younger son of John Glasgow, merchant and burgess/guild brother (p.450, PDF 460). The first entry strongly identifies the maintained John-1348/Helen Smith household; the sons are supported comparisons with Alexander-971 and John-1355. The sons’ entries do not name their mother, and the three admissions must not be treated as a literal statement that all three men form one family. These are inspected published register transcriptions; the underlying manuscript admission registers are unread. Burke’s Visitation, vol.2, printed armorial section p.67 (PDF 341), has now been read in the scan. It explicitly describes Alexander of Old Court, formerly Auchinraith, as eldest son of the late John Glasgow and Helen, daughter of James Smith, and grandson of Alexander Glasgow, merchant, and Agnes Monro of Edinburgh. The family passage was already quoted in the held biography; inspecting it is not discovery of a previously unknown grandfather name. The underlying Lyon matriculation remains unread. Burke names Agnes Monro, not the documented Mary Munro of Alexander-1309’s couple. Their identity cannot be assumed, and the 1771 child has no inspected occupation, wife or estate bridge identifying him as the merchant rather than the Colinton account John-1304. The merchant’s circa 1770 birth is an inherited estimate, not independent corroboration. Retain both modern Johns and the current father selection, all mothers, vital fields and upstream grades. No new father attachment or merge follows. The 1741 childhood identification of Alexander-1309 is not certified by this review. Exact percentages are subjective judgements, not measured probabilities.
